bill.title: Combating Organized Retail Crime Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill directly addresses organized theft targeting retail operations and e-commerce platforms.
The bill explicitly covers theft from interstate and foreign shipments, affecting logistics and shipping companies.
The bill addresses online marketplaces and social media platforms where stolen goods are sold, potentially creating new compliance obligations.
The bill expands money laundering statutes to cover prepaid cards and gift cards, affecting payment processors and card issuers.

bill.plainSummary: This bill expands federal authority to prosecute organized retail theft and supply-chain crime. It allows prosecutors to aggregate the value of stolen goods over a 12-month period to meet felony thresholds, makes these offenses predicate crimes for money laundering charges, and authorizes asset forfeiture. The bill also creates a temporary coordination center within the Department of Homeland Security to help federal agencies work together on these cases.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine and Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; The 'Omnibus' Low NOx Regulation; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects heavy-duty trucking by determining whether stricter California emission standards apply to commercial vehicles and engines.
The bill affects manufacturers of heavy-duty vehicles and engines by determining whether they must comply with California's stricter NOx emission requirements.
Stricter emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles could affect demand for diesel fuel and related petroleum products.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn an Environmental Protection Agency decision that allowed California to enforce stricter pollution standards for heavy-duty trucks and engines than federal law normally permits. The EPA had granted California a waiver to implement its "Omnibus Low NOx" regulation, which sets tougher limits on nitrogen oxide emissions from vehicles. If this resolution passes, that waiver would be nullified and California would be blocked from enforcing those stricter standards.

industries.rationale: The resolution would reopen approximately 48% of the National Petroleum Reserve to oil and gas leasing, directly expanding access for extraction companies.
The resolution removes wildlife and subsistence protections established in the 2022 plan, affecting conservation and indigenous-rights advocacy organizations.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would nullify a 2022 Bureau of Land Management plan that closed roughly 48% of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska to oil and gas leasing in order to protect wildlife and subsistence resources. If enacted, the resolution would revert to a 2020 plan that allowed more of the reserve to be leased for oil and gas development. The reserve is an approximately 23-million-acre area on Alaska's North Slope.

industries.rationale: The resolution directly affects oil and gas leasing rights and acreage availability in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge Coastal Plain.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would overturn a December 2024 Bureau of Land Management decision that restricted oil and gas leasing in Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. The 2024 rule made about 1.2 million acres unavailable for leasing while keeping the legally required minimum of 400,000 acres open. If this resolution passes, it would nullify that restriction and potentially allow the earlier 2020 decision—which opened all 1.6 million acres to leasing—to govern instead.

bill.title: Fair Access to Banking Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates how banks and credit unions may deny financial services to customers.
Digital asset firms have frequently reported being denied banking services, making them likely beneficiaries of fair-access requirements.
Firearms businesses have reported service denials from banks citing reputational risk, which this bill would prohibit.
Cannabis and related businesses have faced banking access challenges that this bill's requirements could address.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would restrict banks, credit unions, and payment card networks from refusing service to customers who comply with the law. Financial institutions could only deny service based on documented, quantitative risk standards set in advance, and could not cite reputational concerns as a reason. Violations would trigger penalties including loss of federal deposit insurance, exclusion from electronic payment systems, and potential civil lawsuits by affected customers.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Consumer Gas-fired Instantaneous Water Heaters".
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 12.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of gas-fired instantaneous water heaters would be directly affected by the nullification of energy efficiency standards that govern their product design and compliance costs.
Natural gas suppliers have a stake in standards that affect the efficiency and market competitiveness of gas-fired appliances versus electric alternatives.
Energy efficiency standards for gas appliances can influence the relative market share of gas versus electric water heating systems.
Contractors and builders who install water heaters would face different product availability and compliance requirements depending on whether the standards remain in effect.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn a Department of Energy rule issued in December 2024 that set new energy efficiency standards for gas-fired instantaneous water heaters (commonly called tankless water heaters). The DOE rule required these appliances to meet stricter energy conservation requirements. If this resolution passes, the new standards would be nullified and would not take effect.

bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 181.

industries.rationale: Land-use restrictions in Alaska's Central Yukon planning area directly affect oil and gas exploration and extraction opportunities on federal lands.
Designations of critical environmental concern areas affect mineral extraction and mining access on the affected federal acreage.
Land-use designations can affect development rights and property values for adjacent or inholding parcels.

The BLM rule designated 21 areas as critical environmental concern or research natural areas. If enacted, the resolution would cancel that rule and restore the prior land-management plan for the region.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Review of Final Rule Reclassification of Major Sources as Area Sources Under Section 112 of the Clean Air Act".

industries.rationale: Industrial manufacturers are frequently classified as major sources of hazardous air pollutants and would face changed regulatory obligations regarding emission controls after reclassification.
Fossil fuel facilities often emit hazardous air pollutants and would be directly affected by changes to emission control requirements when reclassifying source status.
Mining and materials processing operations can be major sources of hazardous air pollutants subject to these reclassification rules.
Waste management facilities may emit hazardous air pollutants and could be affected by changes to emission control requirements during source reclassification.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would nullify an EPA rule that requires industrial facilities to maintain strict emission controls when they reduce their pollution output enough to reclassify from "major source" to "area source" status under the Clean Air Act. The EPA rule was designed to prevent facilities from increasing emissions of persistent and bioaccumulative hazardous air pollutants after reclassifying to the less stringent area source category. If this resolution passes, facilities that reclassify would no longer be required to continue using the emission control methods that were mandatory when they were classified as major sources.

bill.title: Laken Riley Act

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new detention mandates on DHS and creates liability exposure for federal agencies, while authorizing state governments to bring suit over immigration enforcement.

The bill creates new grounds for state litigation against the federal government and expands detention requirements, generating demand for legal services in immigration and intergovernmental litigation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security to detain certain non-citizens who are in the country unlawfully and have been arrested for or charged with crimes including burglary, theft, assault on law enforcement, or offenses causing death or serious injury. It also allows state governments to sue the federal government if immigration enforcement decisions or failures—such as releasing detainees, not conducting required asylum interviews, or violating parole limitations—cause harm to the state or its residents, including financial harm exceeding $100.

bill.title: Stop Russian Market Manipulation Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

industries.rationale: The bill directly restricts imports of eight specific metals and minerals, affecting companies that source, process, or trade these materials.
Manufacturers that rely on platinum-group metals, nickel, copper, or zinc as inputs would face supply-chain changes and potentially higher costs.
Defense contractors use platinum-group metals and specialty alloys in aerospace and weapons systems, making supply sourcing relevant.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would ban the import of eight minerals—platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, nickel, copper, zinc, and braggite—if they are produced in Russia or by Russian entities. The ban would also cover minerals obtained through swaps or other arrangements designed to evade the restriction. The prohibition would remain in effect until one year after the President certifies that Russia has ended hostilities against Ukraine, and would resume if Russia restarts hostilities within three years.

bill.title: HALT Fentanyl Act

industries.rationale: The bill changes registration and licensing requirements for pharmaceutical researchers conducting controlled substance research and affects the regulatory classification of chemical substances.
The bill establishes new criminal penalties and quantity thresholds that will affect prosecution and defense of drug trafficking cases.
Universities and research institutions conducting controlled substance research would be subject to the new registration processes and requirements established by the bill.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would permanently classify all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I controlled substances, meaning they would be treated as having high abuse potential and no accepted medical use. It sets the same criminal penalties and quantity thresholds for fentanyl-related substances as currently apply to fentanyl analogues. The bill also creates a streamlined registration process for researchers studying Schedule I substances and relaxes some requirements for research facilities working with controlled substances.

bill.title: Protecting Access for Hunters and Anglers Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects manufacturers and sellers of lead ammunition by limiting federal authority to regulate their products on public lands.
Manufacturers of fishing tackle containing lead would face fewer potential federal restrictions on their products' use.
Sporting goods retailers selling lead ammunition and tackle would benefit from reduced regulatory uncertainty around these product lines.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prevent three federal agencies—the Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Land Management, and Forest Service—from banning or regulating the use of lead ammunition or fishing tackle on federal lands and waters. The agencies could still impose restrictions in specific locations if they determine, based on field data from that site, that lead use is the primary cause of a wildlife population decline and the state agrees to the regulation. Certain existing regulations would remain in place.

bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 474.

Counties with significant federal land often host mining operations on those lands, and changes to local revenue formulas may indirectly affect permitting and local fiscal capacity.
Federal lands in small counties frequently include oil, gas, or coal extraction sites, and local revenue changes may affect the fiscal environment for these operations.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would modify federal payments to local governments that contain tax-exempt federal land. Specifically, it appears to adjust the Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILT) formula for small counties, which compensates localities for property-tax revenue they cannot collect on federally owned land. Without access to the bill text, the precise nature of the change to the formula or eligibility criteria cannot be described.

bill.title: Veterans 2nd Amendment Protection Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Hearings held. Hearings printed: S.Hrg. 119-35.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects the National Instant Criminal Background Check System used by licensed firearm dealers and importers.
Organizations focused on Second Amendment rights and veterans' advocacy have a direct stake in policies governing firearm access for veterans.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prevent the Department of Veterans Affairs from sending information about veterans or their beneficiaries to the national firearm background-check database solely because they have someone appointed to manage their benefits. districtAwards.description: STATE OF ALASKA RURAL HEALTH TRANSFORMATION PROGRAM - DESCRIPTIVE TITLE: ALASKA’S RURAL HEALTH TRANSFORMATION PROGRAM  ORGANIZATION NAME: STATE OF ALASKA DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH   SUBRECIPIENTS/SUB-AWARDEES: A WIDE RANGE OF ENTITIES ACROSS ALASKA WILL PARTICIPATE AS FUNDING SUBRECIPIENTS, INCLUDING: HEALTH CARE DELIVERY ORGANIZATIONS; TRIBAL HEALTH ORGANIZATIONS; COMMUNITY-BASED ENTITIES; EDUCATION AND WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT INSTITUTIONS; TECHNOLOGY AND INNOVATION VENDORS; PROVIDER AND TRADE ASSOCIATIONS; CONSULTING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICES FIRMS; AND STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS OR AUTHORITIES ENGAGED IN PUBLIC HEALTH, EDUCATION, OR EMERGENCY MEDICAL RESPONSE.   PROJECT GOALS:    1. PROMOTE LIFELONG HEALTH AND WELL-BEING FOR RURAL, REMOTE, AND FRONTIER ALASKANS.    2. BUILD SUSTAINABLE, OUTCOMES-DRIVEN HEALTH SYSTEMS.    3. DRIVE WORKFORCE AND TECHNOLOGY INNOVATION.    TOTAL BUDGET AMOUNT: $1,000,000,000.00    BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FUND USAGE: ALASKA PROPOSES TO USE RHTP FUNDING TO STRENGTHEN COMMUNITY-LED AND REGIONALLY DESIGNED HEALTH SYSTEMS THAT PROVIDE ACCESS TO A FULL CONTINUUM OF CARE AS CLOSE TO ALASKANS’ HOMES AS POSSIBLE. THE FUNDS WILL BE AWARDED TO ENTITIES TO LAUNCH PROJECTS IN SUPPORT OF ALASKA’S SIX INITIATIVES: (1) HEALTHY BEGINNINGS, WHICH STRENGTHENS MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH AS A FOUNDATION FOR HEALTHY FAMILIES; (2) HEALTH CARE ACCESS, WHICH EXPANDS AND SUSTAINS ESSENTIAL PRIMARY, BEHAVIORAL, ORAL, SPECIALTY, EMERGENCY, HOME AND COMMUNITY-BASED AND POST-ACUTE CARE HEALTH SERVICES ACROSS ALASKA’S RURAL COMMUNITIES; (3) HEALTHY COMMUNITIES, WHICH INVESTS IN ENHANCING ACCESS TO PREVENTIVE AND PRIMARY CARE SERVICES THAT ENABLE EARLY CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT, EXPANDING THE USE OF CONSUMER-FACING DIGITAL TOOLS AND POPULATION HEALTH CLINICAL INFRASTRUCTURE, AND PROMOTING HEALTHY LIFESTYLES WITH CULTURALLY APPROPRIATE COMMUNITY EDUCATION; (4) PAY FOR VALUE: FISCAL SUSTAINABILITY, WHICH INCENTIVIZES A SHIFT FROM TRADITIONAL VOLUME-BASED REIMBURSEMENT MODELS TO BUILD THE LONG-TERM FINANCIAL STABILITY OF RURAL PROVIDERS THROUGH VOLUNTARY INNOVATIVE CARE AND PAYMENT MODELS THAT INCREASE CARE COORDINATION, LOWER COSTS AND IMPROVE HEALTH OUTCOMES; (5) STRENGTHEN WORKFORCE, WHICH BUILDS A RESILIENT RURAL HEALTH CARE WORKFORCE THROUGH PIPELINE, RECRUITMENT, TRAINING AND RETENTION STRATEGIES, ALONGSIDE WRAPAROUND HOUSING AND CHILD CARE SUPPORTS TO HELP PROVIDERS REMAIN IN RURAL COMMUNITIES; AND (6) SPARK TECHNOLOGY AND INNOVATION, WHICH HARNESSES DATA AND TECHNOLOGY TO EXPAND THE USE OF CONSUMER WEARABLES AND DIGITAL DEVICES, ENHANCE TELEHEALTH, FOSTER APPROPRIATE USE OF AI, STRENGTHEN CYBERSECURITY, FACILITATE DATA SHARING AND SYSTEM INTEROPERABILITY, AND TEST NEW DELIVERY MODALITIES USING EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES. THESE SIX INITIATIVES ARE FLEXIBLE, PHASED, AND VOLUNTARY, ALLOWING EACH COMMUNITY AND PROVIDER TO ENGAGE AT A PACE AND SCALE SUITED TO THEIR LOCAL PRIORITIES AND RESOURCES. THESE INITIATIVES WILL TRANSFORM ALASKA’S HEALTH SYSTEM. THEY REFLECT ALASKA’S CULTURE OF INNOVATION AND SELF-RELIANCE, AND AFFIRM OUR COMMITMENT TO HIGH-QUALITY, ACCESSIBLE, AND SUSTAINABLE CARE.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
